questions.stem: A 41 year old woman had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 months ago. Since then she has vomited most meals and lost 18 kg. Over 4 days she has become muddled and unsteady on her feet. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She has horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based gait. Capillary glucose is 5.4 mmol/L and CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
questions.e: Vomiting and malabsorption after gastric bypass deplete thiamine, giving confusion, ataxia and nystagmus. A normal CT and glucose make the distractors unlikely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Persistent vomiting and malabsorption after bariatric surgery, then **confusion, ataxia and nystagmus**: thiamine deficiency without alcohol.

elim: CT head is normal, and a bleed would not explain months of vomiting and weight loss.
No liver disease, jaundice or asterixis is described.
Her capillary glucose is normal at 5.4 mmol/L.
B12 deficiency develops over months to years and causes dorsal column loss, not acute confusion and nystagmus.

steps.x: **E. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Malabsorption, starvation and vomiting cause Wernicke's too; alcohol is only the commonest cause.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after being found wandering outside a pub. He drinks 2 bottles of wine a day. He is disorientated in time and place and walks with a wide-based, staggering gait. His pulse rate is 100 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and capillary glucose 6.1 mmol/L. The doctor examines his eye movements.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on eye examination?
o: Right ptosis with a fixed dilated pupil
questions.e: Nystagmus is a common eye sign in Wernicke's encephalopathy alongside ophthalmoplegia. Papilloedema and pupil abnormalities point to other diagnoses.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on eye examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Heavy drinker with **confusion and ataxia**: Wernicke's until proven otherwise. The common eye finding is nystagmus.

elim: A sign of raised intracranial pressure, not thiamine deficiency.
Points to optic nerve disease such as optic neuritis.
Suggests opioid toxicity or a pontine lesion.
A third nerve palsy, classically compressive from an aneurysm.

steps.x: **B. Horizontal nystagmus.** Nystagmus is the commonest eye sign; ophthalmoplegia (for example bilateral lateral rectus palsy) completes the triad.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man who drinks 12 cans of strong cider a day is admitted with a chest infection. On day 2 the nurse notes he is confused and keeps forgetting where he is. He is not tremulous or sweating. His eye movements are full, but he is unsteady when walking. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Only around 10% of patients have all three triad features, so confusion and ataxia in a heavy drinker is enough to suspect Wernicke's. He has no signs of withdrawal and normal glucose and CT.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 12 cans of strong cider a day
confused and keeps forgetting where he is
steps.x: Alcohol, **confusion and unsteadiness** with normal glucose and CT. Normal eye movements do not exclude it.

elim: A gradual decline over years, not an acute change on day 2 of an admission.
Capillary glucose is normal.
CT head is normal.
He is not tremulous, sweating or tachycardic.

steps.x: **D. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Only about 10% have the full triad, so treat confusion with ataxia in a drinker as Wernicke's and give IV thiamine.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man had an episode of confusion and unsteadiness 8 months ago and left hospital before treatment. He still drinks heavily. He is alert and orientated in person only. When asked what he did this morning, he describes in detail a trip to the seaside that did not happen. He cannot recall three words after 5 minutes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on further cognitive assessment?
questions.e: Untreated Wernicke's progresses to Korsakoff's syndrome, with amnesia and confabulation (filling memory gaps with invented stories). Fluctuating consciousness suggests delirium instead.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on further cognitive assessment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: describes in detail a trip to the seaside that did not happen
steps.x: Untreated Wernicke's, then **amnesia** with **invented memories**: Korsakoff's syndrome.

elim: A language deficit from a dominant frontal lesion; his speech is fluent and detailed.
Typical of delirium; he is alert.
Inability to recognise faces, from occipitotemporal damage.
Suggests Lewy body dementia.

steps.x: **A. Confabulation.** Korsakoff's = anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation, after untreated Wernicke's.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is seen in the memory clinic. He has drunk a litre of spirits a day for 30 years and was never treated for any alcohol-related illness. He cannot remember conversations from earlier in the day or events from recent years, and fills the gaps with stories. His gait and eye movements are normal. His attention and language are intact.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Korsakoff's syndrome is the chronic result of untreated Wernicke's, with amnesia and confabulation but preserved attention. Wernicke's itself is acute with confusion, ataxia and eye signs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: a litre of spirits a day for 30 years
cannot remember conversations from earlier in the day
gait and eye movements are normal
steps.x: Chronic heavy drinking, **anterograde and retrograde amnesia** and **confabulation**, with no acute signs.

elim: Causes gradual global decline with language and visuospatial problems, not isolated amnesia with confabulation in a heavy drinker.
Attention is intact and the onset is not acute.
Usually stepwise decline with vascular risk factors and focal signs.
The acute phase with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia; his gait and eyes are normal.

steps.x: **C. Korsakoff's syndrome.** Wernicke's is the acute, treatable phase; Korsakoff's is the chronic amnestic end point.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man is transferred from prison to hospital on day 40 of a hunger strike, taking only water. He has become confused and unsteady over 3 days and complains of double vision. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. He has bilateral failure of abduction of the eyes and nystagmus. Capillary glucose is 4.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying deficiency?
questions.e: Prolonged starvation depletes thiamine (vitamin B1), causing Wernicke's encephalopathy with the full triad here. B12 deficiency develops over years and does not cause acute ophthalmoplegia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying deficiency? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Prolonged **starvation**, then **confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia**: Wernicke's encephalopathy.

elim: B12 deficiency takes years to develop and causes neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration, not acute ophthalmoplegia.
Causes megaloblastic anaemia, not an acute triad of confusion, ataxia and eye signs.
Pellagra causes dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.
B6 deficiency causes neuropathy and sideroblastic anaemia.

steps.x: **E. Thiamine.** Thiamine (B1) stores last only a few weeks, so starvation causes Wernicke's quickly.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man is admitted confused and ataxic, with bilateral lateral rectus palsy, and is diagnosed with Wernicke's encephalopathy. He says he eats a normal diet and takes no regular medicines. He has palmar erythema and spider naevi. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his thiamine deficiency?
questions.e: Chronic alcoholism is the most important cause of Wernicke's encephalopathy. Raised GGT, macrocytosis and liver signs point to it here.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his thiamine deficiency? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Stigmata of chronic liver disease, **raised GGT** and **macrocytosis**: chronic alcohol excess.

elim: Can cause malabsorption, but the liver signs and blood results point to alcohol.
Associated with B12 deficiency, not thiamine deficiency.
Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor causes B12, not B1, deficiency.
Linked to B12 deficiency; thiamine is plentiful in plant foods.

steps.x: **A. Chronic alcohol excess.** Chronic alcoholism is the most important cause of Wernicke's.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by police, who found him slumped in a shop doorway and assumed he was drunk. He drinks heavily every day. He is confused and cannot stand without support. His breath alcohol is zero. His pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg and capillary glucose 6.3 mmol/L. He has nystagmus on lateral gaze. CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Confusion and unsteady gait in a heavy drinker who is not intoxicated is the signature emergency presentation of Wernicke's and needs immediate IV thiamine. A zero breath alcohol rules out intoxication.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: confused and cannot stand without support
steps.x: A drinker who is **confused and ataxic** but **not intoxicated**: the key emergency to recognise.

elim: His breath alcohol is zero.
No jaundice, ascites or asterixis is described.
CT head is normal.
No seizure, tremor or autonomic overactivity is described.

steps.x: **D. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Never assume a confused, unsteady drinker is just drunk; give IV thiamine.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman who drinks heavily is admitted with vomiting and a capillary glucose of 2.6 mmol/L. She is treated with intravenous 10% glucose, followed by 5% glucose infusions for 24 hours. No vitamins are prescribed. The next day she is newly confused and cannot walk unaided, and has bilateral lateral rectus palsies. CT head is normal and glucose is 6.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Glucose given without thiamine to a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. Central pontine myelinolysis follows rapid sodium correction, not glucose.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Glucose given to a heavy drinker **without thiamine**, then confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.

elim: Caused by over-rapid correction of hyponatraemia, not glucose.
Would cause tremor, hallucinations and autonomic overactivity, not ophthalmoplegia.
Her glucose is 6.8 mmol/L.
Her hypoglycaemia was corrected quickly and does not explain bilateral sixth nerve palsies.

steps.x: **E. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's; always give Pabrinex with glucose in drinkers.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with alcohol dependence is admitted confused and ataxic, and is started on intravenous Pabrinex for Wernicke's encephalopathy. He also complains of burning feet for several months. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. The doctor examines his legs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his legs?
o: Bilateral extensor plantars with brisk reflexes
Proximal muscle weakness with normal sensation
Reduced sensation in a stocking distribution
Unilateral foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum
questions.e: Peripheral neuropathy commonly accompanies Wernicke's encephalopathy, giving symmetrical distal (stocking) sensory loss. Upper motor neurone signs point elsewhere.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his legs? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Wernicke's commonly comes with **peripheral neuropathy**: burning feet and symmetrical distal sensory loss.

elim: Upper motor neurone signs, not a peripheral neuropathy.
Mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs suggest motor neurone disease.
Suggests a myopathy.
A single common peroneal nerve palsy, not a symmetrical neuropathy.

steps.x: **D. Reduced sensation in a stocking distribution.** Commonly: nystagmus, short-term memory loss and peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man who drinks heavily is admitted confused and unsteady. He complains of double vision that is worse when looking to either side. Neither eye moves outward past the midline. Vertical eye movements are normal and his pupils react normally. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Dysfunction of which cranial nerves best explains his eye signs?
questions.e: Failure of both eyes to abduct is bilateral lateral rectus palsy, supplied by the abducens (VI) nerves: the classic ophthalmoplegia of Wernicke's. Third nerve palsy would affect the pupil and lid.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Dysfunction of which cranial nerves best explains his eye signs? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: worse when looking to either side
Neither eye moves outward past the midline
steps.x: Failure of **abduction** in both eyes = bilateral lateral rectus palsy = sixth nerve.

elim: Would cause ptosis, dilated pupils and failure of adduction and vertical gaze.
Affect vision and pupil reactions, not eye movements.
Cause vertical diplopia, worse looking down and in.
Supplies facial muscles, not eye movement.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral abducens nerves.** Ophthalmoplegia in Wernicke's is classically bilateral lateral rectus (abducens) palsy.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has gastric cancer causing gastric outlet obstruction. She has vomited daily for 3 weeks and is on intravenous fluids awaiting a stent. She becomes confused and unsteady and has nystagmus. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. CT head shows no metastases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged vomiting and poor intake deplete thiamine and cause Wernicke's encephalopathy. Normal sodium, calcium, urea and CT exclude the distractors.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Weeks of **vomiting** and no oral intake, then **confusion, ataxia and nystagmus**, with normal metabolic tests.

elim: CT head shows no metastases.
Her calcium is normal.
Her sodium is normal.
Her urea is normal.

steps.x: **E. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Think Wernicke's in any malnourished or vomiting patient who becomes confused and ataxic, not only drinkers.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with alcohol dependence is admitted confused and ataxic with ophthalmoplegia. He refuses treatment and leaves hospital against medical advice. His GP is worried about what will happen if the condition is not treated.
questions.q: Which is the most likely long-term complication if he remains untreated?
questions.e: Without thiamine, Wernicke's encephalopathy progresses to Korsakoff's syndrome, with irreversible amnesia from mamillary body and thalamic damage.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely long-term complication if he remains untreated? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Untreated **Wernicke's** progresses to a chronic amnestic state.

elim: Follows over-rapid correction of hyponatraemia.
Causes gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and dementia; not linked to thiamine deficiency.
A neurodegenerative movement disorder unrelated to thiamine.
An inherited disorder of copper metabolism.

steps.x: **B. Korsakoff's syndrome.** Untreated Wernicke's leads to Korsakoff's syndrome with permanent amnesia and confabulation.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man who drinks heavily is admitted confused and ataxic with nystagmus. Capillary glucose is 6.0 mmol/L and CT head is normal. The foundation doctor asks how the diagnosis of Wernicke's encephalopathy is confirmed.
questions.q: Which is the gold standard for diagnosing this condition?
o: Clinical diagnosis from history and examination
questions.e: The gold standard for Wernicke's is clinical diagnosis. MRI may support it but is not required, and thiamine levels are not used acutely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the gold standard for diagnosing this condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A drinker with **confusion, ataxia and nystagmus**: the diagnosis is made at the bedside.

elim: CSF is normal in Wernicke's; it is used to look for infection or bleeding.
May support the diagnosis but is not required.
Measures folate stores, not thiamine.
Not routinely used acutely; results are slow and would delay treatment.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis from history and examination.** Wernicke's is a clinical diagnosis; MRI may support it and thiamine levels are not used acutely.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 14 kg/m². She becomes confused and unsteady with nystagmus. Capillary glucose is 4.8 mmol/L. The foundation doctor wants to send a blood thiamine level and wait for the result before prescribing.
questions.q: Which investigation result is needed before starting specific treatment?
questions.e: Wernicke's encephalopathy is diagnosed clinically and IV Pabrinex should be given immediately. Thiamine levels are not used acutely and waiting risks permanent damage.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation result is needed before starting specific treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: wait for the result before prescribing
steps.x: Clinical picture of **Wernicke's** in a malnourished patient. The test would only delay treatment.

elim: A research-style test of thiamine status; it would delay urgent treatment.
Supportive only; never delay thiamine for imaging.
Not relevant to thiamine deficiency.
Not routinely used acutely; waiting risks progression to Korsakoff's.

steps.x: **C. None; treat on clinical suspicion.** Wernicke's is a clinical diagnosis: give IV Pabrinex straight away.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with alcohol dependence is treated with intravenous Pabrinex for confusion and ataxia. Her eye movements were normal and the team wants more support for the diagnosis, so an MRI brain is arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely MRI finding?
o: Bilateral symmetrical high signal in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal grey
Crescentic extra-axial collection over one hemisphere
questions.e: MRI in Wernicke's supports the diagnosis by showing symmetrical changes in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal grey, which have high metabolic turnover. Temporal lobe signal suggests HSV encephalitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely MRI finding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
MRI **supports** Wernicke's by showing damage where metabolic turnover is highest.

elim: Describes a subdural haematoma.
Typical of multiple sclerosis.
Suggests abscess or tumour.
Typical of herpes simplex encephalitis.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral symmetrical high signal in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal grey.** MRI changes in Wernicke's are in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal grey.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man sees his GP with poor memory and falls. His wife is worried about his drinking but he says he is a social drinker. Examination is normal apart from a mildly unsteady gait. The GP wants to screen for alcohol dependence.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The CAGE questionnaire is the first-line screen for alcohol dependence. A blood alcohol level only shows recent intake.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The question asks for a **screen for alcohol dependence**.

elim: A cognitive screen, not an alcohol dependence screen.
Shows only recent intake, not dependence.
Not a screening test for alcohol dependence.
Screens for depression.

steps.x: **C. CAGE questionnaire.** CAGE: Cut down? Annoyed? Guilty? Eye-opener? is the first-line alcohol dependence screen in the notes.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman is recovering from Wernicke's encephalopathy on the ward. Before discharge she completes the CAGE questionnaire. She says people annoy her by criticising her drinking and that she has a drink first thing in the morning to steady her nerves. She has not felt she should cut down and does not feel guilty.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of her CAGE result?
o: Score of 2, diagnostic of liver cirrhosis
questions.e: She scores 2 (Annoyed and Eye-opener), which is clinically significant for alcohol dependence. CAGE is a screening tool and does not assess liver damage.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of her CAGE result? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: annoy her by criticising her drinking
drink first thing in the morning
not felt she should cut down
steps.x: Yes to **Annoyed** and **Eye-opener**, no to Cut down and Guilty.

elim: She answered yes to two questions.
She answered yes to Annoyed and Eye-opener, which is 2.
CAGE screens for dependence; it says nothing about liver damage.
She answered no to Cut down and Guilty.

steps.x: **D. Score of 2, suggesting alcohol dependence.** A CAGE score of 2 or more is clinically significant and suggests dependence; refer for alcohol support.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man is on day 2 of an admission for alcohol withdrawal and is taking chlordiazepoxide. He becomes newly confused and cannot walk to the toilet without help. He has nystagmus. His pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg and capillary glucose 5.9 mmol/L. He has no tremor or hallucinations.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus in a drinker needs immediate IV thiamine (Pabrinex). Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed and is used for prevention, not treatment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
New **confusion, ataxia and nystagmus** in a drinker, without signs of withdrawal.

elim: He has no tremor or hallucinations; more sedation will not treat thiamine deficiency.
Treats agitation, not the cause, and lowers the seizure threshold in withdrawal.
Oral absorption is poor in drinkers; established Wernicke's needs parenteral thiamine.
Low dose oral vitamins do not treat acute Wernicke's.

steps.x: **C. Intravenous Pabrinex.** Suspected Wernicke's = IV Pabrinex now; oral thiamine is for prevention, not treatment.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man with alcohol dependence was started on oral thiamine 100 mg three times a day by his GP. A week later he is brought in confused, with an ataxic gait and bilateral lateral rectus palsy. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and capillary glucose 6.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue oral thiamine at the same dose
Intravenous Pabrinex as a single dose
questions.e: Confirmed Wernicke's encephalopathy needs parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) for 5 days. Oral thiamine is unreliable in drinkers and a single dose is not enough.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: oral thiamine 100 mg three times a day
steps.x: The full **triad** despite oral thiamine: he now has established Wernicke's.

elim: He has developed Wernicke's despite it; oral absorption is unreliable.
Glucose without thiamine can worsen Wernicke's.
Confirmed Wernicke's needs parenteral thiamine for 5 days, not one dose.
Does not treat thiamine deficiency.

steps.x: **D. Intravenous Pabrinex for 5 days.** Established Wernicke's: parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) for 5 days.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man who drinks heavily is found at home with a GCS of 11. His capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L. He is unsteady and has nystagmus. Pabrinex is not stocked in the Emergency Department and pharmacy says it will take an hour to arrive. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride until Pabrinex arrives
Intravenous 20% glucose now, with Pabrinex as soon as it arrives
Withhold glucose until Pabrinex has been given
questions.e: Correcting hypoglycaemia takes priority, so give IV 20% glucose now and Pabrinex as soon as it is available. Withholding glucose risks hypoglycaemic brain injury.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate immediate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Severe hypoglycaemia** with reduced GCS in a drinker who may have Wernicke's.

elim: Delays correcting hypoglycaemia, and glucagon works poorly when glycogen stores are low in drinkers.
Does not correct the hypoglycaemia.
Unsafe with a GCS of 11.
Hypoglycaemia can cause permanent brain damage; correcting it takes priority.

steps.x: **C. Intravenous 20% glucose now, with Pabrinex as soon as it arrives.** Hypoglycaemia first: never delay glucose for thiamine. Give Pabrinex alongside or as soon as possible.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man who drinks 80 units of alcohol a week is nil by mouth after an emergency laparotomy. He is alert and orientated. A maintenance infusion of 5% glucose with potassium is planned. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which should be given before the glucose infusion is started?
questions.e: Glucose uses up thiamine, so in a heavy drinker IV Pabrinex is given before glucose-containing fluids. He is nil by mouth, so oral thiamine is not possible.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which should be given before the glucose infusion is started? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **heavy drinker** about to receive **glucose**: protect him from precipitated Wernicke's.

elim: He is not hypoglycaemic, and more glucose without thiamine increases risk.
Chlordiazepoxide is given orally for withdrawal and does not protect against Wernicke's.
He is nil by mouth.
He is not diabetic or hyperglycaemic.

steps.x: **C. Intravenous Pabrinex.** In anyone at risk of thiamine deficiency, give thiamine before or with glucose.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted with tense ascites. She drinks a bottle of wine a day and has lost weight. She is alert and orientated with a normal gait and eye movements. After paracentesis she is to be discharged with alcohol team follow-up.
questions.q: Which vitamin treatment is most appropriate on discharge?
questions.e: Oral thiamine is recommended for harmful drinkers who are malnourished or have decompensated liver disease. IV Pabrinex is for suspected Wernicke's, which she does not have.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which vitamin treatment is most appropriate on discharge? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Harmful drinking with **malnourishment** and **decompensated liver disease**, no Wernicke's signs.

elim: Treats B12 deficiency, which is not suggested here.
Used for suspected or confirmed Wernicke's; she has no neurological signs.
She has decompensated liver disease and malnourishment, so she needs thiamine.
Not the priority in preventing Wernicke's.

steps.x: **D. Oral thiamine.** Oral thiamine for harmful drinkers who are malnourished, have decompensated liver disease or are in assisted withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has completed 5 days of intravenous Pabrinex for Wernicke's encephalopathy. His confusion and nystagmus have improved. He is underweight and wants to stop drinking. He is reviewed before discharge.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Oral thiamine, nutritional support and alcohol cessation
questions.e: After the IV course, long-term management is oral thiamine, nutritional support and treating the cause with alcohol cessation. Benzodiazepines are not continued long term.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate long-term management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Acute treatment done. Now **prevent recurrence**: thiamine, nutrition and the underlying cause.

elim: Does not address his nutrition or thiamine stores.
Parenteral thiamine is a short course; long-term thiamine is oral.
Benzodiazepines are only for short-term withdrawal; long-term use causes dependence.
He remains at high risk while malnourished and drinking.

steps.x: **E. Oral thiamine, nutritional support and alcohol cessation.** Long term: oral thiamine, nutritional support and alcohol cessation.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant has hyperemesis gravidarum and has vomited for 5 weeks. She is admitted with ketonuria and becomes confused with nystagmus and an unsteady gait. Capillary glucose is 4.4 mmol/L. Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose is prescribed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
o: Intravenous Pabrinex before the glucose-containing fluid
questions.e: Hyperemesis gravidarum can cause Wernicke's, and glucose without thiamine can worsen it, so give IV Pabrinex before the glucose-containing fluid. Oral thiamine is not enough with neurological signs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: confused with nystagmus and an unsteady gait
steps.x: Prolonged **vomiting** in pregnancy, **Wernicke's signs**, and glucose about to be given.

elim: Treats the vomiting but not the thiamine deficiency.
Does not treat Wernicke's.
Too late and unreliable; she has established neurological signs.
Not indicated; Wernicke's is treated with thiamine.

steps.x: **B. Intravenous Pabrinex before the glucose-containing fluid.** Give IV thiamine before glucose in anyone at risk of thiamine deficiency.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with alcohol dependence has Wernicke's encephalopathy. A biochemistry lecturer explains that thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for enzymes of glucose metabolism, including one in the pentose phosphate pathway that is measured in red cells as a test of thiamine status.
questions.q: Which enzyme is the lecturer describing?
questions.e: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase, the pentose phosphate pathway enzyme. Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which enzyme is the lecturer describing? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Thiamine-dependent enzyme in the **pentose phosphate pathway**.

elim: The first pentose phosphate enzyme, but it uses NADP, not thiamine.
Phosphorylates glucose and does not need thiamine.
